Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Ravi, a 37-year-old psychologist, had always been deeply invested in understanding the human condition, but ever since the terror attack that shattered his sense of safety, he found himself grappling with a reality that felt increasingly alien. The day of the attack had begun like any other; he had gone to his favorite café in downtown San Francisco, a place he frequented with his wife, Aditi. They had just finished a leisurely brunch when the unmistakable sound of gunfire erupted outside. It shattered the morning calm, plunging the bustling street into panic. As he dove for cover, the chaos around him seemed to warp time and space, each moment stretching into an eternity. The screams, the frantic footsteps, and the acrid smell of gunpowder filled his senses, leaving an indelible mark on his psyche.

In the months that followed, Ravi’s world transformed. What once felt like a vibrant and hopeful existence began to morph into a landscape dominated by anxiety and fear. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, ripe with threats lurking just beyond the edges of his awareness. At work, he found himself increasingly on edge, often feeling like an imposter in his own practice. He had dedicated his life to helping others navigate their traumas, yet he felt profoundly helpless against his own. The very idea of being unable to control what happened to him was suffocating; he was no longer the confident clinician who could guide his patients through darkness. Instead, he felt like a shadow of his former self—unrecognizable and lost.

Ravi’s nights became a battleground. He dreaded the dark, fearing he would wake up to the echoes of gunfire that haunted him. Each time he stirred from slumber, his heart raced, and the room felt as if it were closing in around him. He avoided going to bed early, choosing instead to stay up late, numb in front of the television, escaping into mindless shows that did little to soothe his racing thoughts. The darkness had become a trigger, a reminder of his vulnerability, and he often lay there, breathless, wishing he could shake the feeling that he was never truly safe.

During the day, he meticulously crafted a facade of normalcy. He avoided anything that could be stressful—social gatherings, crowded places, and even conversations about current events. Friends and colleagues grew concerned, noticing that he had become increasingly withdrawn. He would often decline invitations to lunch or coffee, preferring to isolate himself in his office, where he felt a semblance of control. But as the weeks turned into months, the isolation began to take its toll on his relationship with Aditi. She often expressed her worries, and while he desperately wanted to reassure her, he felt that any attempt to articulate his fears would only deepen her concern. He had come to believe that sharing his experiences would make her feel helpless too, and he could not bear the thought of adding to her burdens.

To cope, Ravi found himself drifting into a world of fantasy, escaping into daydreams where the gunfire never existed, and he was simply a man living a peaceful life. Alcohol became a nightly companion, dulling the edges of his anxiety and providing a brief respite from the reality he could no longer bear. He would sip whiskey in solitude, the warmth in his chest a fleeting comfort, but he knew it was a hollow victory—a temporary escape that left him feeling even more disconnected from who he once was.

The turning point came unexpectedly when he attended a professional conference and was met with a colleague who, noticing his state, asked him directly about his well-being. Ravi felt exposed in that moment, but something in the sincerity of the inquiry pierced through his defenses. He found himself articulating the fears he had kept bottled up—the feeling of helplessness, the dread of the dark, and the disorientation that had become his constant companion. As he spoke, he realized he could no longer navigate this storm alone. The recognition of his struggles, both by himself and by another, ignited a flicker of hope. It prompted him to seek help, to reclaim not just his identity as a psychologist but as a man, a husband, and a citizen of a world that, despite its dangers, still held the potential for healing and connection.

Now, as he sits in the therapist's office, Ravi's heart is heavy with uncertainty. He hopes for understanding, for a way to tether himself back to the life he once cherished. But beneath that hope lies a fear that lingers—a fear that this journey may not lead him back to the man he used to be, but to a new version of himself, one forever changed by the echoes of gunfire that still haunt him.
